Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

# 1 Samuel 1 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records the family background of Samuel, Hannah's barrenness and suffering, her prayer and vow at Shiloh, the birth of Samuel, and his dedication to the Lord. The traditional reading sees this as God raising up a transitional figure — Samuel, last of the judges and first of the prophets — out of a godly family living amid the moral chaos of the late Judges period.

**Sources:** EnduringWord.com (David Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic), PreceptAustin.org (compilation of Spurgeon, Wiersbe, Bergen, etc.), Gill's Exposition (Baptist/Reformed), Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican), Pulpit Commentary, NET Bible notes (modern scholarship).

---

## v. 1 — Elkanah's Lineage and Home

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"A certain man"**: God's typical method is to find a person He can use and work through him. This "certain man" (Elkanah) is the pivot point for God's next great work — raising up Samuel. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Ramathaim-zophim**: Literally "the double height of the watchers." It is almost certainly the same place later called simply Ramah (v. 19). The dual form "Ramathaim" likely refers to a town built on two hills. "Zophim" (watchers) may refer to watchtowers or to descendants of Zuph. (PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary; Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Elkanah was a Levite** of the family of Kohath (cf. 1 Chronicles 6:22–28, 33–38), though here called an Ephraimite/Ephrathite because his family resided within the tribal territory of Ephraim, and Levites were reckoned by the tribe where they lived. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"Ephrathite"** is rightly translated "Ephraimite" here and should not be confused with "Bethlehemite" (as in Ruth 1:2). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Spurgeon** (Baptist): "On how small an incident the greatest results may hinge! The pivots of history are microscopic." He notes that the smallest trifles are arranged by the God of providence as much as the most startling events. (PreceptAustin.org citing Spurgeon, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)

- **The "hill country of Ephraim"** is the same phrase that introduced two of the most sordid tales in Judges (Judges 17:1; 19:1). Into this moral cesspool, God introduces a godly family, especially a godly mother, Hannah — much as the book of Ruth brought light into the dark days of the Judges. (PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible):**

- The NET notes that the LXX reads "a man from Ramathaim, a Zuphite," and the MT reading "Zophim" may have arisen from dittography (accidental doubling of a letter). (NET Bible, https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8)

---

## v. 2 — Two Wives: Hannah and Peninnah

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Polygamy** was a fact of life in the ancient world, but the Bible never presents it in a favourable light. Strife and conflict always characterise polygamous families in Scripture. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **Hannah** means "grace" or "graciousness"; **Peninnah** means "coral," "ruby," or "red pearl." Hannah is mentioned first, suggesting she was the first wife, and that Elkanah took Peninnah because of Hannah's barrenness (cf. Genesis 16:2–3; 30:3–4, 9). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)

- **Gill** (Baptist/Reformed): Though polygamy was connived at, it was contrary to the original law of marriage; Elkanah, though a good man, was chastised for it with much family vexation. Hannah's barrenness was not natural but specifically because the Lord had shut her womb, to prompt her to pray and to make Samuel's birth more remarkable. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that polygamy was a licence permitted to the Jews but not generally indulged in except by kings. In Christianity it was marked for final extinction by the rule that no polygamist should even be admitted to the diaconate (1 Timothy 3:2, 12). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## v. 3 — Yearly Pilgrimage to Shiloh

**Traditional Reading:**

- Elkanah went up **yearly** (likely at one of the three annual feasts, probably Passover) to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was. Though the Law commanded three appearances a year, by this period even devout Israelites typically went once annually — a practice that continued into New Testament times (Luke 2:41). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **"LORD of Hosts" (Jehovah Sabaoth)**: This is the **first occurrence** of this divine title in Scripture, though it appears about 260 times in total. It means "LORD of Mighty Armies," referring not primarily to military armies but to the innumerable hosts of heaven — the stars, the angels — over which God rules. Its origin may lie in a period of struggle between star-worship and Hebrew monotheism; the title is a protest against idolatry, claiming God's dominion over the heavenly bodies. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **Hophni and Phinehas** are mentioned by name because they were notoriously wicked priests (see 1 Samuel 2:12–17, 22–25). Their mention highlights Elkanah's godliness: the wickedness of the priests did not make his own worship invalid, nor did he use it as an excuse to stay away. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Eli** had devolved his priestly functions to his sons while he discharged only the duties of judge. He was a man of statesmanlike ability who had brought prosperity and subdued the Philistines, yet he failed in his own household. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

**Jewish Tradition (via Gill):**

- The Talmud notes that from the day God created the world, no one called Him "Lord of hosts" until Hannah came and called Him so. (Gill citing Talmud Beracot 31.2, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## vv. 4–5 — The Double Portion

**Traditional Reading:**

- At the ceremonial meal following the peace offering, Elkanah distributed portions to his family. To Peninnah and each of her children he gave a portion; to Hannah he gave a **"worthy portion"** or "double portion" (Hebrew *appayim*, literally "one portion of two faces"). This public gesture displayed his special love for Hannah. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html; EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **"The LORD had closed her womb"**: The Hebrew verb suggests God "shut up" or restrained her. The trial of barrenness was under God's sovereign control, part of His purpose to accomplish something great through Hannah and to further the whole plan of salvation. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Pulpit Commentary** notes an alternative reading: the Septuagint has a different Hebrew original (*epes* for *apaim*), which would yield "to Hannah he gave one portion only" (since she had no children to receive portions). The Vulgate took *apaim* as "anger," rendering "Elkanah was sad when he gave Hannah her portion." However, the traditional "double portion" reading is preferred by most English translations. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

**NET Bible (Modern Scholarship):**

- The exact sense of *appayim* ("two faces") is uncertain. It is most likely a portion double the normal amount. Evidence for this use derives primarily from Aramaic rather than Hebrew, but it fits the context. Some scholars have followed the LXX emending the word to *epes* ("but" or "however"). (NET Bible, https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8)

---

## vv. 6–7 — Peninnah's Provocation

**Traditional Reading:**

- Peninnah is called Hannah's **"rival"** or "adversary" (Hebrew *tsaratah*). She "provoked her severely" — the Hebrew can carry the sense of thundering against her, being loud and clamorous with reproaches and scoffs. Polygamy poisoned the entire home life. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- The provocation happened **"year by year"** at the very time when the family went up to the house of the LORD. Peninnah chose the solemn occasion of the feast to taunt Hannah, probably insinuating that her barrenness was a sign of God's curse. This made Hannah weep and refuse to eat — she could not enjoy even the double portion of her husband's love. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html; EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Pulpit Commentary** notes a textual issue: the Hebrew consonants can be read either "and so he did" (referring to Elkanah) or "and so she did" (referring to Peninnah). The ancient versions (LXX, Syriac, Vulgate) translate "she did," which makes better sense contextually. The Masoretic vowel pointing (added centuries later) read it as "he did." (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Precept Austin** (Handfuls of Purpose): Peninnah's taunts served to drive Hannah into the place of blessing. "We may thank God for the trials that send us into His presence." (PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)

---

## v. 8 — Elkanah's Insensitive Comfort

**Traditional Reading:**

- Elkanah genuinely loved Hannah, but his attempt at comfort — **"Am I not better to you than ten sons?"** — was insensitive. He did not recognise that she had deep needs he could not fulfil, particularly the desire for motherhood, which for a Hebrew woman carried special significance including the hope of being ancestress of the Messiah. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- The number **ten** is used, like seven, as an ideal or round number in the OT (cf. Daniel 1:20, Zechariah 8:23). Jarchi notes that Peninnah had borne Elkanah ten sons. (NET Bible notes, https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8; Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## v. 9 — Hannah Rises; Eli at the Doorpost

**Traditional Reading:**

- After the sacrificial meal, Hannah rose and went to pray. **Eli the priest** (the high priest) was seated on a chair (or "pontifical throne") by the doorpost (Hebrew *mezuzah*, indicating a porch or entrance structure) of the "temple" (Hebrew *heykal*, "palace") of the LORD. The tabernacle is here called a "temple," showing this term was in use before Solomon's building. Solid structures had grown up around the tabernacle during its ~300 years at Shiloh. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Gill** notes that according to Jewish tradition, none but kings of David's line might sit in the court of the tabernacle; Eli sat at the entrance gate. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## vv. 10–11 — Hannah's Prayer and Vow

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"In bitterness of soul"**: Hannah was deeply distressed — not only from barrenness but from years of taunting. Yet she did the right thing: she took her bitter and anguished feelings to God in honest, fervent prayer. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **"O LORD of Hosts"**: Hannah called on God as the "LORD of Mighty Armies" because she felt attacked by her rival and needed a protector. This illustrates how believers may address God by the name or title that matches their circumstance. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **The vow had two parts**: (1) The son would be given to the LORD **all the days of his life** — beyond the normal Levitical service, which was from age 30 to 50 (Numbers 4:2–3). (2) **"No razor shall come upon his head"** — a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), making Samuel a lifelong Nazirite. This was extremely rare; Samson (Judges 13:5) and John the Baptist (Luke 1:15) were similarly consecrated. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Hannah's humility**: She calls herself God's "handmaid" three times in this verse, and the threefold "look… remember… not forget" shows the intensity and importunity of her prayer. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- The Nazirite vow involved: (a) abstinence from any grape product, signifying distance from fleshly pleasures; (b) no contact with the dead, showing higher concerns than ordinary joys and sorrows; (c) uncut hair, a public visible sign of consecration. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

**Jewish Tradition (via Gill):**

- The Talmud (Beracot 31.2) says Hannah was the first person to call God "Lord of hosts." A tradition in Mishnah Sotah 3.8 debates whether a woman could vow her son as a Nazirite; some held that only a man could. However, Samuel was universally regarded as a perpetual Nazirite. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## vv. 12–14 — Eli Misjudges Hannah

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"As she continued praying"**: literally "as she multiplied to pray." Only a summary of her long prayer is recorded. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Silent prayer**: Hannah was "speaking in her heart" — her lips moved but no voice was heard. This shows that effective, prevailing prayer does not need to be vocal; it can be silent and inward. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Eli's misjudgment**: Eli "watched her mouth" and, seeing her quivering lips, flushed face, and prostrate form, concluded she was drunk. The Pulpit Commentary suggests that silent prayer may have been unusual at that time — it requires "a certain advance in civilisation and refinement" and strong faith to believe God hears silent utterances. Eli's suspicion also reflects poorly on the religious atmosphere at Shiloh: drunkenness at the fellowship meals may have been common. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Clarke** (cited by Guzik): "The fact that Eli supposed her to be drunken… prove that religion was at this time at a very low ebb in Shiloh; for it seems drunken women did come to the place." (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **Ellicott** notes that the LXX attempts to soften the harshness by inserting "servant" before Eli, suggesting an attendant spoke the harsh words. But the Hebrew text clearly has Eli himself speaking. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

---

## vv. 15–16 — Hannah's Humble Reply

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"No, my lord"**: Though falsely accused, Hannah responded with remarkable modesty and humility. Calvin remarked: "Consider the modesty of Hannah, who, though she had received injury from the high priest, yet answers with reverence and humility." (Ellicott citing Calvin, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"Poured out my soul before the LORD"**: This is exactly what Hannah needed to do. Instead of keeping the bitterness inside, she poured it out before God — an act of honest, transparent prayer. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **"A daughter of Belial"**: The Hebrew *Belial* means "worthlessness." A "daughter of worthlessness" means a wicked or worthless woman. It was not yet a proper name for Satan (as in 2 Corinthians 6:15). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **"Out of the abundance of my complaint and grief"**: Her long prayer was not vain repetition but the overflow of deep anguish. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## vv. 17–18 — Eli's Blessing; Hannah's Faith

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant your petition"**: Eli may have intended this only as a kind wish, but it was in fact a **word from the LORD** — something like the unconscious prophecy of Caiaphas in John 11:51. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Hannah's countenance changed immediately**: She received Eli's word **with faith**. "Her face was no longer sad" — the change in her expression shows she believed the promise before any physical evidence. Hebrews 6:12 commends those who "through faith and patience inherit the promises." (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **She ate**: Hannah returned to the sacrificial feast and participated in it. Having cast her burden on the LORD, her spirit was relieved. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

**Handfuls of Purpose (Precept Austin):**

- "It is one thing to tell the Lord about our burdens; it is quite another thing to cast them on the Lord. The countenance is sure to be changed when the heart has found rest in the will of God." (PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-commentary-handfuls-of-purpose-james-smith)

---

## vv. 19–20 — Samuel's Birth

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Early morning worship**: Before returning home, the family rose early to worship the LORD — a repeated pattern in this family (see vv. 3, 19, 28). Hannah worshipped in faith while the promise was still unfulfilled. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **"The LORD remembered her"**: "Remembered" is an anthropomorphism — it is not as though God had forgotten Hannah, but it describes God now acting on His knowledge to fulfil His purpose. The phrase echoes God's "remembering" of other barren women in Scripture (Sarah, Rachel). (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **"In the course of time"**: Literally "in the process of time." It did not happen immediately. Hannah had to wait, making her an example of those who "through faith and patience inherit the promises" (Hebrews 6:12). (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

- **The name "Samuel"** (Hebrew *Shemuel*): The traditional explanation is "heard of God" or "name of God." Hannah's explanation — "Because I have asked for him from the LORD" — is not a literal etymology but a wordplay. The Hebrew for "asked" (*sha'al*) sounds like the first part of Samuel. The name is a living testimony that God heard and answered her prayer. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

---

## vv. 21–23 — Hannah Waits to Wean Samuel

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Elkanah and his house went up** for the annual sacrifice — and **"to fulfill his vow"**: This indicates Elkanah had also made a vow concerning the child, ratifying Hannah's vow and adding a thank-offering of his own. Vows were characteristic of the age of the Judges (cf. Jephthah, Samson). (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html; Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

- **Weaning**: In ancient Near Eastern culture, weaning typically occurred around age two or three (2 Maccabees 7:27 mentions three years). Hannah's delay was not reluctance but practical care, and perhaps an unhurried treasuring of her time with the child. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"Only may the LORD confirm His word"**: Elkanah spoke wonderful counsel — "do everything in obedience to God so we may see His word established." The "word" may refer to Eli's pronouncement in v. 17, which Elkanah recognised as carrying divine authority. There is also an ancient rabbinic tradition that a "Bath-kol" (heavenly voice) announced a coming righteous one named Samuel, and that Elkanah's prayer references this. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html; Rashi cited in Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm)

---

## vv. 24–25 — Presentation at Shiloh

**Traditional Reading:**

- **The offerings**: "Three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine." The BSB reads "a three-year-old bull" (following the LXX and some Hebrew manuscripts), while the Masoretic Text reads "three bulls." The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott explain that one bull was for the burnt offering of consecration for Samuel; the other two were for the regular festival offering. The ephah of flour (about 22 litres) corresponds to the prescribed grain offering for three bulls (Numbers 15:8–10). (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"The child was young"**: Samuel was perhaps three years old — old enough to be weaned, yet young enough to be called a "child" (Hebrew *na'ar*). (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

---

## vv. 26–28 — Hannah's Testimony and Dedication

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"As surely as you live, my lord"**: This oath formula ("as your soul lives") is peculiar to the Books of Samuel (occurring six times) and once in Kings. The similar formula "as the LORD lives" is frequent in Judges–2 Kings, and this reflects the age of vows and oaths. (Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"I am the woman who stood here beside you praying"**: Hannah gave a simple, powerful testimony — she who once prayed in anguish now stood with the answer in her arms. (PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)

- **"I now dedicate the boy to the LORD"** (BSB); more literally "I have lent him to the LORD" (KJV). The Pulpit Commentary notes that "lent" is a false rendering; the Hebrew verb (*sha'al*) is the same root as "asked." The sense is: "The LORD gave him to me, and now I have returned him whom I obtained by prayer to the LORD, as one asked or demanded." It does not suggest Hannah "owned" him and "lent" him; rather, he is her answered prayer given back to the Giver. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/1.htm; Ellicott, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

- **"So they worshiped the LORD there"**: Worship is a repeated characteristic of this family (vv. 3, 19, 28). Even in the painful act of leaving their young son at the tabernacle, they worshipped. This is a "sacrifice of praise" (Hebrews 13:15). (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Because this chapter is predominantly narrative, major doctrinal disputes are limited. However, some distinctives emerge:

**Reformed / Calvinist (e.g., Calvin, Spurgeon):**
- Strong emphasis on **God's sovereignty** over Hannah's womb: "the LORD had closed her womb" and "the LORD remembered her." The trial was not random; God ordained the barrenness for a greater redemptive purpose — raising up Samuel. (Calvin's Commentaries via BibleHub; Spurgeon via PreceptAustin.org, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-1-commentary)
- Calvin praises Hannah's modesty before Eli as an example of godly submission, even when falsely accused — a Reformed emphasis on humility and deference to authority. (Ellicott citing Calvin, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-1.html)

**Baptist (e.g., Gill):**
- Gill emphasises that polygamy was **contrary to the original creation ordinance** (cf. Matthew 19:8; Malachi 2:15). Though a "good man," Elkanah was chastised for his sin through family discord. This reflects the historic Baptist conviction that Scripture consistently condemns polygamy as sin, even in the patriarchs. (Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/1.htm)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (e.g., David Guzik / Enduring Word):**
- Guzik emphasises **prevailing prayer** and the immediate, faith-filled change in Hannah's countenance after receiving God's word. He highlights that "prevailing prayer doesn't need to be vocal; effective prayer can be silent and in the heart" — a point relevant to charismatic practice of both vocal and silent prayer. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)
- The use of God's covenant name "LORD of hosts" is presented as something believers can intentionally choose to match their circumstance — a "name it and claim it" approach to God's names rather than material blessings. (EnduringWord.com, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-1/)

**Lutheran:**
- No distinctively Lutheran sources were retrieved for this chapter within the allowed sites (lcms.org, 1517.org).

**Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness:**
- No distinctively Methodist sources were retrieved for this chapter within the allowed sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com). However, the emphasis on Hannah as a model of consecration ("as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD") resonates with Holiness teaching on entire sanctification and total dedication to God.

---

## Other Views: Modern Scholarship and Catholic/Orthodox

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible / bibleodyssey.org):**

- The NET Bible notes several **text-critical issues**:
  - **v. 1**: The MT "Zophim" may originate from dittography (accidental letter-doubling); the LXX reads "a Zuphite." (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8)
  - **v. 5**: The word *appayim* ("two faces") is uncertain; the translation "double" draws on Aramaic usage more than Hebrew. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8)
  - **v. 7**: The MT has "he did" (masculine), but context suggests Peninnah (feminine). The NET follows the Syriac Peshitta in reading a feminine verb. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Samuel+1:1-8)

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **God works through ordinary people** in dark times — Elkanah and Hannah were faithful amid national corruption.
2. **Barrenness as divine purpose**: Hannah's suffering was neither random nor punishment, but part of God's redemptive plan.
3. **Honest, persistent prayer**: Hannah models pouring out one's soul before God without pretence.
4. **Faith receives God's word before seeing results**: Her countenance changed immediately after Eli's blessing.
5. **Costly dedication**: Hannah gave back to God the very gift she most desired — a pattern of true worship.
